original_summary: Put is an old two-to-four-player trick game with 3 cards each and the odd rank order 3-2-A-K-...-4. Players do not have to follow suit, and winning 2 of 3 tricks scores a point. At any moment a player may call 'Put' to stake the whole game, and the opponent must fold (conceding 1) or 'see it'. The previously tested two-player variation, 'Put: Trick by Trick', used a simultaneous PUT / HOLD-AND-SEE / HOLD-AND-FOLD call before trick 1 and again before trick 2, a raised stake of 3, and 24 hands.

review.evidence: Always-PUT forces every hand to stake 3 at the first call, so the second call never happens. The thoughtful player's only levers are a blind fold-or-see and a near-random 3-card allocation. Correct play gains only about +0.25 per hand, about +6 over 24 hands, against a match spread of about 10. Always-PUT therefore still wins roughly 25-30% of matches. No seat has an edge, but a thoughtless policy is far too competitive.

When both players play sensibly, the decisive points come from stake-3 showdowns between two hands both players liked. These are settled by which 3 random cards are stronger. The test estimates that chance decides 40-50% of matches.

There is little to improve on beyond a fold threshold of about the bottom 30% of hands. Allocation of 3 cards in simultaneous play adds about +0.05 per hand. A weak player can score, but a strong one has almost no further levers.

Cards are hidden, but the first call is simultaneous, so there is no betting sequence to read. The trick-1 card that could inform the second call is seen only when nobody put at call 1, which a PUT-heavy opponent prevents. Bluffing and opponent reading barely move the score.
Tricks, stakes, points and hands won are all arithmetic. No judge is needed.
It is two-player, turn-based and text-only, with one deal per hand. It uses 4 choice steps at most and stays within the step limits.

problems: P1: Always-PUT is too strong. Because the first call is simultaneous, putting blind cannot be punished by a re-raise, and it wins about 25-30% of matches against correct play.
P2: The deal dominates. Stake-3 showdowns between two strong hands decide most matches, and about 40-50% of results are chance.
P3: Inference is thin. A simultaneous first call gives no betting sequence to read, no information is public before betting, and the second call is usually skipped.
P4: Card play is nearly skill-free. With 3 cards and nothing to choose except the order, the stronger hand wins its tricks almost regardless.
P5: The match is too short. 24 hands cannot let a per-hand skill edge outweigh the variance.

changes.what: The betting becomes a sequence with a re-raise. The caller, who alternates each hand, says PUT or PASS. The responder answers a PUT with SEE, FOLD or RE-PUT, and answers a PASS with PUT or PASS. The caller then answers a RE-PUT, or a PUT made after their PASS, with SEE or FOLD.
changes.why: A blind putter can now be re-put by a strong hand and must then fold, costing 2, or see at stake 4. Calls are made in order, so they can be read and bluffed.

changes.what: The stakes are rescaled: 1 if nobody puts, 2 if a PUT is seen, 4 if a RE-PUT is seen. A fold to a PUT pays the putter 1, and a fold to a RE-PUT pays the re-putter 2.
changes.why: The ladder rewards value-raising strong hands against a player who never folds, and makes well-timed bluffs and folds worth real points. Against always-PUT, folding the bottom ~37% of hands and re-putting the rest yields about +0.56 per hand.

changes.what: Each player is dealt 4 cards. The 4th is face up, visible to both, and the other 3 are private. A player plays only 3 of the 4 cards and chooses which to leave out.
changes.why: The public card gives each player something to infer the opponent's strength and calls from. Choosing which card to drop, and in what order to play the others, against a known opponent card adds decisions to the card play. Every bet is judged against visible information.

changes.what: Card play becomes a single simultaneous secret submission of an ordered list of 3 cards. Trick 1 is the first card of each list, and so on.
changes.why: This keeps the original's free play of any card while fitting the 4-choice limit next to three betting steps. Ordering against a known face-up card is a guessing game in which reading the opponent pays.

changes.what: The match lasts 40 hands instead of 24, with the caller alternating so each player calls 20 times.
changes.why: Estimated edge against always-PUT is about +22 points against a spread of about 20 over 40 hands, which puts the thoughtless policy near or below a 13% win rate. The reasoner-vs-reasoner edges from reading and bluffing also accumulate.

changes.what: The original rule is restored that a hand is scored only by a player who wins at least 2 of the 3 tricks. Trick-and-tie, or one trick each with a tie, scores nothing.
changes.why: This is faithful to the original and makes the choice of order matter. A weaker hand that forces ties can neutralise a big stake.

keeps: The rank order 3-2-A-K-Q-J-10-9-8-7-6-5-4, with suits irrelevant.
Any card may be played, with no need to follow suit.
Equal ranks tie a trick, which belongs to no one.
Winning 2 of 3 tricks scores the hand, and trick-and-tie scores nothing.
The 'Put' call that raises the stake, answered by 'I see it' or by folding and conceding.
Three-card hands in play and an alternating first player.

recommendation.reason: The Put/see/fold core is a compact bluffing game. A betting sequence with a re-raise, a public card, a choice of which card to drop, and a longer match fix the failures within the limits.

variation.name: Put: Show One, Keep Three
variation.summary: A two-player bluffing card duel over 40 hands. Each player holds 4 cards, one of them face up. Players bet in sequence (PUT, SEE, FOLD, RE-PUT) on a best-of-3-tricks showdown played with 3 of their 4 cards in a secretly chosen order.
variation.rules:
CARDS. Use a standard 52-card deck; suits do not matter. Strengths: 3 = 13, 2 = 12, A = 11, K = 10, Q = 9, J = 8, 10 = 7, 9 = 6, 8 = 5, 7 = 4, 6 = 3, 5 = 2, 4 = 1. Higher strength is better.

SETUP. There are two players, A and B. Each starts with 0 points and 0 hands won. The match lasts exactly 40 hands. In odd-numbered hands A is the Caller and B the Responder. In even-numbered hands B is the Caller and A the Responder.

EACH HAND:
1. Deal. Shuffle all 52 cards and deal 4 cards to each player. Each player's 4th card is face up and announced to both players. The other 3 are private to their holder.

2. Caller's call. The Caller says PUT or PASS.

3. Responder's answer.
- If the Caller said PUT, the Responder says SEE, FOLD or RE-PUT. On SEE, the stake is 2; go to step 5. On FOLD, the Caller scores 1 point and wins the hand; go to step 8. On RE-PUT, go to step 4.
- If the Caller said PASS, the Responder says PUT or PASS. On PASS, the stake is 1; go to step 5. On PUT, go to step 4.

4. Caller's answer. This step happens only if the Responder said RE-PUT or PUT in step 3. The Caller says SEE or FOLD.
- After a RE-PUT: SEE makes the stake 4. FOLD gives the Responder 2 points and the hand.
- After a PUT that followed the Caller's PASS: SEE makes the stake 2. FOLD gives the Responder 1 point and the hand.
- A FOLD ends the hand; go to step 8.

5. Play (simultaneous). Each player secretly writes an ordered list of 3 different cards chosen from their own 4 cards. The face-up card may be used or left out. The lists are then revealed.

6. Tricks. Compare the 1st cards of the two lists, then the 2nd cards, then the 3rd cards. In each pair the higher strength wins that trick. Equal strength ties the trick, and it belongs to no one.

7. Score. A player who won at least 2 of the 3 tricks scores the stake (1, 2 or 4) and wins the hand. Otherwise, for example one trick each with a tie, or one win and two ties, or three ties, nobody scores.

8. Announce. Announce all calls, all 8 cards (including any card that was left out or never played), the hand result, and both players' points and hands won.

END. After hand 40 the match ends.
variation.objective: After 40 hands, the player with more points wins. If points are equal, the player with more hands won wins. A hand is won by scoring it on tricks or by the opponent folding. If both are equal, the match is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Always-PUT is now punished. A reader re-puts the top ~60% of hands and folds the rest cheaply, for an estimated edge of about +0.56 per hand, about +22 over 40 hands against a spread of about 20. That leaves the blind policy winning roughly 10-13% of matches. Always-SEE loses to value raises, and always-PASS or always-FOLD lose outright. Between two reasoners, the visible card and the order of calls give something to read. A PASS from a Caller showing a 3 is suspicious, and a RE-PUT against a high face-up card signals strength or a bluff. Folds at 1 or 2 points and value raises to 4 now shift the score as much as raw card strength does. Choosing which card to leave out, and how to order the rest against a known enemy card, rewards anticipating the opponent's order. Equal-rank ties let a weaker hand void a big stake. This is a two-player zero-sum duel, so talk is omitted: it would add nothing beyond what the calls already signal.

balanced.evidence:
SEATS. The 12 hands are an even number and the Opener alternates, so each seat opens 6 hands and any edge from move order cancels. The deck and the deal are symmetric.

STAKES:
- No Put: 1 point.
- Put then Fold: the putter scores 1.
- Put then See: 3 points to the player who won more tricks, 0 if trick counts are equal.

The labels match the numbers.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (by the winner rule):
(a) Always Put / always See.
- Against an always-See random player, the stake is always 3 and the result follows the deal. That is about 50/50, so the policy does not dominate.
- Against a sensible player, the sensible player Folds weak hands (-1) and Sees strong ones. On a strong hand the expected value of Seeing is about +3 x P(win | strong) - 3 x P(lose | strong). The sensible player comes out ahead, so the policy loses often.
(b) Always Fold. This concedes 1 point every time the opponent Puts. An opponent who always Puts wins by about +6 or more, so this policy loses.
(c) Always Pass / never Put. The opponent can Put strong hands and gain 3 against your See, or 1 against your Fold. This policy loses on average.
(d) Always order cards strongest first. An opponent who expects this places the weakest card first. They then take tricks 2 and 3 with middle-vs-weak and strong-vs-middle. The policy is exploitable, not dominant.

CONCLUSION. No option is strictly better whatever the opponent does. Every policy can lose, and both players can realistically win.

One concern, not a failure: hands with tied trick counts score 0 and point totals are small, so drawn matches will be fairly common.

playable.evidence:
CALL SEQUENCE. It is complete:
- Opener Put leads to Responder See or Fold.
- Opener Pass, then Responder Put, leads to Opener See or Fold.
- Both Pass gives stake 1.
- Equal ranks tie a trick, and equal trick counts score nothing.

ENGINE FIT. The arrangement step is a simultaneous poll over the 6 orderings, which the engine supports. The game is finite (12 hands) and decided by arithmetic on scores.

LIMITS:
- Choice steps: 4 (opener call, responder call, answer, arrangement), which is at the limit.
- Steps: 15, within 20.
- Attributes: 13, within 20. That is enough for 6 card strengths, 2 scores, the stake, the opener and trick tallies.
- Hidden elements: 1, within 3.
- Random draws: 1 shuffle per round.
- Rounds: 12, within 40.

Dealing from a shared deck uses the remove/append workaround, which costs steps but fits.

OTHER CHECKS. There are two players, so the talk question does not arise. No board, judge or clock is needed. It is not an iterated cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT WAS LOST. The original game's skill lay in sequential trick play. A player leads, sees the reply, decides whether to sacrifice a low card, and can Put mid-hand after seeing tricks. The variation replaces this with one blind simultaneous ordering, made before any of the opponent's cards are seen.

THE ORDERING SUBGAME. Each player knows only their own 3 cards, so ordering is a 6x6 guessing game against unknown cards. Its equilibrium is mixed. For most hands the trick result therefore depends on the deal plus a near-coin-flip guess.

DOMINATED HANDS. When one hand beats the other card by card after sorting, which happens in a large share of deals, ordering does not matter at all and the deal decides the hand outright.

WHAT INFERENCE REMAINS. The only real inference left is the Put/See/Fold signal, which is one bluff-or-call decision per hand.

SENSIBLE PLAY BY BOTH. Take sensible play to mean: Put strong hands, See medium-strong ones, and order at random. The hand result is then set by card strength plus ordering luck. Over 12 hands with stakes of 1 or 3, the variance in deal quality is large compared with the small expected edge from better Put/See decisions.

ESTIMATE. About 65-75% of match outcomes are decided by the deal and blind ordering. A player who reasons well is only weakly favoured, and chance alone often decides the winner.

required_changes: Restore information during play so that reasoning matters. Play the 3 tricks one at a time as simultaneous single-card polls, and reveal both cards after each trick, so later tricks are planned from what has been revealed.

To stay within 4 choice steps, merge the calls into ONE simultaneous poll before trick 1. Each player picks Pass-and-Fold-to-Put, Pass-and-See, or Put. Resolve the poll arithmetically: Put vs Fold gives the putter +1 and the hand ends; Put vs See or Put vs Put gives stake 3; any other pair of Pass answers gives stake 1. The 3 trick polls then make 4 choice steps.
Lengthen the match to 24-30 hands (within the 40 limit) so that deal variance averages out and better Put/See and trick decisions decide the winner.
Optionally break ties in total points by the number of hands won, to reduce the frequency of drawn matches.

balanced.evidence:
SEATS: every call and both choice tricks are simultaneous, so neither seat moves first or sees more. The only asymmetry in the original, the non-dealer lead, is gone. No seat edge.

FIRST-CALL TABLE. Payoff to Row. E is Row's expected trick margin at stake 1, from -1 to +1, which depends on the hands.
Row PUT  vs Col PUT: 3E | vs Col SEE: 3E | vs Col FOLD: +1
Row SEE  vs Col PUT: 3E | vs Col SEE: E  | vs Col FOLD: E
Row FOLD vs Col PUT: -1 | vs Col SEE: E  | vs Col FOLD: E
The second call has the same shape after trick 1, but a fold there pays 2 instead of 1.

DOMINANCE: there is none.
- PUT against SEE: they differ only when Col sees (3E against E) or folds (+1 against E). PUT is worse whenever E<0 and Col sees.
- FOLD against SEE: they differ only when Col puts (-1 against 3E). Folding is right exactly when E<-1/3.
- SEE is never dominated: it is the best answer to PUT when E>-1/3.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, by the winner rule:
- Always FOLD. It loses every hand to a putter (-1 per hand, -24 over the match). It loses.
- Always SEE. Every hand plays out, at stake 3 if Col puts, and Col puts selectively. Its expected result is negative and it loses most matches.
- Always PUT. Against always-FOLD it wins 24-0. Against always-SEE every hand is a random stake-3 hand, so about 50/50. Against sensible play it loses on average (see reasoning_over_luck), but it often wins.
- Random play. Random folds to a Put cost 1, and random Puts on weak hands cost 3E. It loses on average.
No policy wins or draws almost every time. Both players can realistically win. A drawn match needs equal points and equal hands won over 24 hands, which is rare. The labelled numbers are consistent: stake 1, raised 3, fold at call 1 pays 1, fold at call 2 pays 2.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS: every case of each call is covered. That is PUT/PUT, PUT/SEE, PUT/FOLD, and 'otherwise' (SEE/SEE, SEE/FOLD, FOLD/FOLD), which keeps stake 1. A FOLD answer only takes effect against a PUT; this is clear, if oddly named. The second call is skipped once the hand is raised. Trick ties and hand ties are defined, and trick 3 is automatic.

FINITE AND ARITHMETIC: exactly 24 hands. Scoring is arithmetic on points kept by the game. The tiebreak is hands won, then a draw.

LIMITS:
- Steps: 14 of 20.
- Choice steps: 4 of 4 (call 1, trick 1, call 2, trick 2).
- Attributes: 14 of 20.
- Hidden elements: 1 of 3.
- Random draws: 1 per round (one shuffle-and-deal).
- Rounds: 24 of 40.
The deal needs the shared_deck_draw workaround and a strength lookup. Both are tight but feasible within 14 steps, using arithmetic `when` conditions for scoring.

NO EXTRAS: no judge, board, clock, trading or binding promises. Two players, so the talk question does not arise. The game is zero-sum, so the late-round cooperation test does not apply. Late hands give the trailing player a real reason to Put and the leader a reason to fold, which is strategic, not degenerate.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
SKILL EDGE AGAINST ALWAYS-PUT. Every hand is raised at call 1, so the second call never happens. The sensible player's only levers are fold-or-see at call 1 and the simultaneous allocation of 3 cards.
- Best response: see when E>-1/3, which is roughly the top 70% of hands, and fold otherwise.
- Folding about 30% of hands costs 0.30 x 1 = -0.30.
- Seeing about 70% of hands, with an average margin of about +0.25 against a random hand, gains 0.70 x 3 x 0.25 = +0.52.
- Allocation skill in a 3-card simultaneous Blotto-like play adds perhaps +0.05.
- Net edge: about +0.25 points per hand, or about +6 over 24 hands.

VARIANCE. About 17 stake-3 hands are played out, each with a standard deviation of about 3 x 0.8 = 2.4. Over the match that is about 2.4 x sqrt(17) = 10 points. With an edge of +6 against a spread of 10, the thoughtless always-PUT player still wins about 25-30% of matches against correct play.

AGAINST A FELLOW REASONER the picture is worse. When both play the intended strategy (put strong, see medium, fold weak), most decisive hands are stake-3 showdowns between hands both players liked. Those are settled by the deal, because the stronger 3-card hand wins its tricks almost regardless of order. Bluffing and inference only shift the occasional 1- or 2-point fold.

THE DEAL DOMINATES. There are 3 random cards per player and swings of 3 points. Within a hand, the result is mostly the deal. Over 24 hands, chance decides a large share of matches, about 40-50% by this estimate.

INFERENCE IS THIN. There is something to infer: the opponent's call pattern, and the trick-1 card before call 2. But call 2 is reachable only when nobody put at call 1, and with a fully simultaneous first call there is no betting sequence to read. A good reasoner is favoured, but not clearly enough.

required_changes: Reduce the share of the result decided by the deal. Deal 5 cards to each player and have each secretly keep 3, so that hand construction is a skill. Alternatively, show one card of each player face up before the first call, so calls can be inferred from.

Make the first call sequential, with a re-raise. For example, the hand's alternating first caller may PUT or PASS. The other then answers SEE, FOLD or RE-PUT (stake 5), and the first caller may then see or fold. This gives bluffing and reading a real betting sequence instead of a blind simultaneous guess.
Lower the swing of showdowns relative to folds. Make a raised stake 2 rather than 3, and a fold at call 1 cost 1, so that well-timed folds and bluffs move the score as much as raw card strength does.

Raise the match to 36-40 hands, within the 40-round limit, so that a per-hand skill edge of +0.25 or more outweighs the variance. The aim is for an always-PUT policy to win under 15% of matches against sensible play.

balanced.evidence:
Seats: there are 40 hands, with A calling in the 20 odd hands and B calling in the 20 even hands. The Responder acts after seeing the Caller's call, but each seat holds that position 20 times. Deals are symmetric, so neither seat has a structural edge.

Decision table. Let w and l be a player's estimated chances of winning and losing the showdown. Ties score 0.
- Facing PUT: SEE = 2(w-l), FOLD = -1, RE-PUT = +2 if the Caller folds or 4(w-l) if the Caller sees. SEE beats FOLD exactly when w-l > -0.5. RE-PUT beats SEE only with a strong hand, or when a bluff makes the Caller fold.
- Caller facing RE-PUT: SEE = 4(w-l), FOLD = -2. Seeing is right only when w-l > -0.5.
- After PASS-PASS: the stake is 1, worth w-l.
- After PASS then PUT: SEE = 2(w-l), FOLD = -1.
No action is best in every case. Each depends on hand strength and on what the opponent's calls reveal.

Thoughtless policies under the WINNER RULE (total points over 40 hands):
(a) Always first option (Caller PUT, Responder SEE, Caller SEE). Every hand is played for stake 2 or 4 whatever the cards. A sensible opponent folds bad hands to the PUT for -1. It re-puts good hands and collects 4 from a weak hand that always sees. It loses showdowns of about 2 to 4 points only when it holds a hand of near-even strength. The policy is net negative against sensible play, and it loses individual hands to random play whenever its cards are worse.
(b) Always PASS/FOLD. It concedes 1 every time the opponent puts. A sensible opponent puts every hand, so this policy loses about 20 to 40 points.
(c) Always highest bid (PUT or RE-PUT, always SEE). This is policy (a) plus RE-PUT. The opponent simply sees with good hands at stake 4, so the policy loses heavily on its bad deals.
None of these policies avoids losing. No option is strictly better whatever the opponent does. Both players can win.

Play phase: using a higher card in a slot is never worse than using a lower card there. Choosing WHICH three cards is therefore weakly dominant: keep the top three. The ORDER of those three (6 permutations against 6) is a real simultaneous matching game. With hands such as 13,10,5 against 11,9,8, the result depends on the order: 13/10/5 vs 11/9/8 gives a win, a win and a loss for the first player. 5/13/10 vs 11/9/8 gives a loss and two wins, so the first player still wins. Other orders, for example 13/5/10 vs 8/11/9, swing the result. No fixed order is dominant.

playable.evidence:
Rules completeness:
- Every call sequence leads to a defined stake or fold result: PUT-SEE gives 2, PUT-FOLD gives +1 to the Caller, PUT-REPUT-SEE gives 4, PUT-REPUT-FOLD gives +2 to the Responder, PASS-PASS gives 1, PASS-PUT-SEE gives 2, PASS-PUT-FOLD gives +1 to the Responder.
- Trick comparison, ties and scoring are fully specified.
- The match winner is decided by points, then hands won, then a draw. All of these are tallies the game keeps.
- Folds count as hands won, and this is stated.

The game is finite: exactly 40 hands, each with at most 3 calls and one play.

Platform limits:
- steps_per_round: 17 (limit 20).
- choice steps: Caller call, Responder answer, Caller answer, play = 4 (limit 4). The play is a simultaneous poll, as required.
- attributes: 17 (limit 20).
- hidden elements: 1, the private cards (limit 3).
- random draws: 1 shuffle and deal per hand (limit 1).
- rounds: 40 (limit 40).
The 3 pairwise comparisons, the trick count and the conditional scoring fit as `when`/`if` arithmetic. No conditional block, board, clock, judge, trading or binding promise is needed.

Talk: two-player zero-sum, so omitting talk is correct. The game is purely competitive, so the cooperation-after-betrayal concern does not apply. Late hands stay contested: up to 4 points can swing per hand, and a trailing player has the re-put to catch up.

Minor wording: 'different cards' means distinct physical cards, so two kings may both be played. This is clear enough.
